## Short version

A TLB is a small CPU cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations. On a big-memory server it covers a tiny share of RAM, so many accesses need a slow page-table lookup. Huge pages make each TLB entry cover 512 times more memory, but they can raise memory use and cause pauses.

All numbers assume x86-64 Linux. The examples use a 512 GiB server and a 2,048-entry TLB, the count on recent Intel server cores [Ref1].

## Words used here

- **Page**: a fixed-size block of memory. The default size is 4 KiB.
- **Virtual address**: the address a program uses.
- **Physical address**: the real location in RAM.
- **Page table**: a tree in RAM that maps virtual pages to physical pages.
- **Page walk**: the CPU reads the page table to find one translation.
- **TLB reach**: the memory that all TLB entries cover together.
- **Huge page**: a 2 MiB or 1 GiB page.
- **THP (Transparent Huge Pages)**: Linux gives huge pages to programs automatically.
- **hugetlbfs**: Linux reserves a fixed pool of huge pages for explicit use.
- **Compaction**: the kernel moves pages to create large free blocks.
- **NUMA (non-uniform memory access)**: each CPU socket has its own nearby RAM.
- **RSS (resident set size)**: the RAM that a process holds now.

## 1. What a TLB is

TLB stands for translation lookaside buffer.

- Every memory access uses a virtual address. The CPU must translate it to a physical address first.
- The page table holds the translation. With 4 KiB pages, a page walk reads 4 levels of the tree.
- The TLB stores the results of recent page walks. A hit skips the walk.
- One TLB entry maps one page of any size.

```
virtual address --> [ TLB ] --hit--> physical address
                       |
                      miss
                       v
                 [ page walk ] ----> physical address
                 (4 table reads)     (result stored in TLB)
```

Insufficient data for your server: I did not read its TLB sizes. `cpuid -1 | grep -i tlb` prints them (`cpuid` is a tool that prints CPU details).

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

1. **The TLB covers very little of the RAM.** Its reach is 2,048 × 4 KiB = 8 MiB, or 0.0015% of 512 GiB. A program that reads large data at random then misses on almost every access.
2. **The page table does not fit in the CPU caches.** Mapping 512 GiB with 4 KiB pages needs 1 GiB of last-level tables. So a page walk often reads from RAM, at about 100 ns per read (est.).
3. **The walk delays the data read.** The CPU cannot fetch the data until it has the physical address. A random access then waits for two RAM reads in sequence instead of one.
4. **Virtual machines make walks longer.** A virtual machine has two page tables: one in the guest and one in the host. One walk can then need up to 24 memory reads [Ref2].
5. **NUMA can make walks slower.** The page table may be located in the RAM of another socket. Each walk step then reads remote RAM.

Cost of one translation, typical values (est.), not measured on your server:

```
one '#' = 20 ns (est.)

TLB hit                |                      0 to 2 ns
walk, tables in cache  |.                     about 10 ns
walk, 1 RAM read       |#####                 about 100 ns
walk, 4 RAM reads      |####################  about 400 ns
```

The CPU also caches the upper levels of the tree. So a typical walk on a big data set costs about 1 RAM read.

One study measured a graph workload on 4 KiB pages. It spent 51% of its CPU cycles on TLB misses. With 2 MiB pages, the share fell to 10% [Ref3].

## 3. How huge pages help

| Page size | TLB reach | Share of 512 GiB | Walk levels | Last-level tables for 512 GiB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KiB | 8 MiB | 0.0015% | 4 | 1 GiB |
| 2 MiB | 4 GiB | 0.78% | 3 | 2 MiB |
| 1 GiB | 1 TiB | 100% | 2 | 4 KiB |

The 1 GiB row assumes 1,024 entries for that page size [Ref1].

- **Fewer misses.** Each entry covers 512 times more memory with 2 MiB pages.
- **Shorter walks.** A 2 MiB page removes one tree level. A 1 GiB page removes two.
- **Cheaper misses.** The tables shrink from 1 GiB to 2 MiB, so they stay in the CPU cache. A miss then costs about 10 ns instead of about 100 ns (est.).
- **Fewer page faults.** One fault maps 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB.

Notes for the review:

- For fully random access over 512 GiB, 2 MiB pages still miss often. The tables now fit in cache, so each miss is cheap.
- The gain is largest for programs that access large data at random. Examples are hash tables, graph traversal and databases.
- Programs that read memory in order gain little.
- In a virtual machine, the guest and the host must both use huge pages for the full gain.

Linux offers two ways to turn huge pages on [Ref4] [Ref5]:

| | THP | hugetlbfs |
|---|---|---|
| Who asks for huge pages | The kernel, automatically | The program or the administrator |
| Page sizes | 2 MiB | 2 MiB and 1 GiB |
| Memory reserved in advance | No | Yes, a fixed pool |
| When no huge page is free | Uses 4 KiB pages, no error | The allocation fails |
| Can be swapped | Yes | No |
| Main setting | `always`, `madvise` or `never` | `vm.nr_hugepages`, or kernel boot parameters |

In `madvise` mode, only regions that the program marks get huge pages. `madvise` is the system call that gives memory hints to the kernel.

## 4. What can go wrong

The detection column uses the kernel counter files `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/vmstat`.

| Problem | Mode | How to detect |
|---|---|---|
| **Memory use grows.** A program touches 1 byte and receives a full 2 MiB page. Sparse data structures can then hold much more RAM [Ref6]. | THP | RSS of the process, `AnonHugePages` in `/proc/meminfo` |
| **Page faults pause the program.** The kernel may run compaction inside a fault to build a free 2 MiB block. The program waits during that work [Ref6]. | THP, mainly with `defrag=always` | `compact_stall` in `/proc/vmstat`, slowest request times |
| **Coverage falls as uptime grows.** Free memory becomes fragmented, and the kernel then uses 4 KiB pages without any error. Identical runs can give different speeds. | THP | `thp_fault_fallback` in `/proc/vmstat` |
| **The pool size must be correct.** A pool that is too large leaves too little RAM for other programs. A pool that is too small makes `mmap` fail with `ENOMEM` [Ref5]. | hugetlbfs | `HugePages_Free` and `HugePages_Rsvd` in `/proc/meminfo` |
| **1 GiB pages need early reservation.** After some uptime, the kernel rarely finds a free contiguous 1 GiB block. Reserve these pages on the kernel command line. | hugetlbfs | `nr_hugepages` reads back lower than requested |
| **Pages land on the wrong NUMA node.** The pool is divided per node. A page on the wrong node makes every access remote. | both | `numastat -p PID`, `/sys/devices/system/node/node*/hugepages/` |
| **`fork()` costs more.** After `fork()`, a write to a shared huge page makes the kernel split or copy it. Programs that save snapshots with `fork()` see pauses and extra memory use [Ref7]. | THP | pauses during snapshots |
| **Allocators conflict with THP.** An allocator frees memory in 4 KiB pieces, which splits huge pages. The kernel may merge them again later, which uses CPU time. | THP | `thp_split_pmd` and `thp_collapse_alloc` in `/proc/vmstat` |
| **The first access is slower.** The kernel must zero the whole page at the first access. That is est. 100 to 200 µs for 2 MiB and est. 50 to 100 ms for 1 GiB. | both | startup time, time of the first pass over a buffer |
| **Settings are system-wide.** The THP mode and the hugetlbfs pool apply to the whole server. On a shared server, a change affects every user. | both | review the change with the other users first |

## 5. A lower-risk way to turn them on

1. Measure the possible gain first. On Intel CPUs, `perf stat -e dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,dtlb_store_misses.walk_active,cycles` gives the share of cycles spent in page walks. That share is roughly the largest gain that fewer TLB misses can give.
2. Start with THP in `madvise` mode. Only the buffers that the program marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages. This limits memory growth to those buffers.
3. Use hugetlbfs, reserved at boot, for large buffers that live for the whole run. Coverage is then guaranteed, so performance is repeatable.
4. Record huge-page coverage with every performance result. Use `AnonHugePages` and `thp_fault_fallback`. Without this record, two runs are not comparable.

## References

I cited these from memory and did not open them in this session. Check the figures from [Ref1], [Ref2] and [Ref3] before you put them on a slide.

- [Ref1] Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Optimization Reference Manual, TLB parameter tables per core generation.
- [Ref2] Bhargava et al., "Accelerating Two-Dimensional Page Walks for Virtualized Systems", ASPLOS 2008.
- [Ref3] Basu et al., "Efficient Virtual Memory for Big Memory Servers", ISCA 2013, table of TLB miss cycles, graph500 row.
- [Ref4] Linux kernel documentation, "Transparent Hugepage Support", https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html
- [Ref5] Linux kernel documentation, "HugeTLB Pages", https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html
- [Ref6] Kwon et al., "Coordinated and Efficient Huge Page Management with Ingens", OSDI 2016.
- [Ref7] Redis documentation, "Diagnosing latency issues", section on transparent huge pages.
